extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical Latin literature (Horace/Satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and practical implications for composing/reading classical Roman satire, especially Horatian satire — form, themes, structure, and devices. Focuses on using dialogue/monologue forms, exempla, moral purpose, and tonal balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue–monologue hybrid form
rubrics_metrics.description: The Satire 'stands midway between dialogue and monologue' and perhaps indicates the author experimenting with form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mixed frame: sustain a long didactic/sermonic passage while enclosing it within a spoken-dialogue framework to provide variety, dramatic interplay, and possible lighter interruptions. The dialogue can serve as an organizing frame for extended reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing with light humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The dialogue-form 'allows the poet to employ a light, humorous vein in both beginning and end, where he turns the laugh against himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance heavy doctrinal or moral argument with a playful opening and closing that undercuts or humanizes the speaker — e.g., self-deprecating jokes or banter — so long exposition is reader-friendly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a representative persona to teach (Ofellus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace 'puts the discourse in the mouth of Ofellus, an old neighbour... a representative of the simplicity and other sturdy qualities of the Apulian farmers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey the poem's moral through a vivid persona whose background and character embody the theme; a plain but shrewd speaker can lend authority and concrete color to abstract precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme illustrated by philosophic commonplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The Satire is 'mainly a collection of commonplaces taken from the teachings of the various philosophic schools' and reproduces ideas from Epicurus and Cicero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground the satirical argument in recognizable philosophical maxims and parallels (explicit or allusive) so the theme gains intellectual weight and resonance with literate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide long sermo into distinct topical parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Stertinius's sermon 'may be divided into four parts, dealing with avarice (82-157), ambition (158-223), self-indulgence (225-280), and superstition (281-295)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting an extended moral critique, structure it into discrete sections each focused on a particular vice or folly, using transitions and exempla to keep the reader oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray striking forms of human folly with exempla
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer's 'main aim throughout is to portray striking forms of human folly' and he does so via illustrative stories (e.g., Oppidius's sons, Nomentanus, lovers, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, often anecdotal examples and named types to exemplify each folly — concrete stories make satire persuasive and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target contemporary manners and philosophical types
rubrics_metrics.description: A second aim is 'to ridicule the airs and manners of the Stoic preachers of the day' and various social behaviours (avarice, ambition, self-indulgence, superstition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select intelligible social or intellectual targets (schools, manners, professions) and satirize their pretensions or excesses so the poem engages with contemporary debate and mores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced moral position — avoid substituting one fault for another
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Plain living is not the same as mean living, and you must not avoid one fault merely to fall into another. There is a happy mean between stinginess and extravagance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present moral counsel with nuance: distinguish moderateness from meanness and practice a 'golden mean' approach rather than advocating austere extremes or naïve remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete everyday detail to illustrate abstract points
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments are illustrated with everyday food, farming, and domestic details (e.g., pullet vs. peacock, bread and salt sufficing after toil, raisins and figs at dessert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete sensory and domestic imagery drawn from ordinary life to dramatize ethical points and to make the satire relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of named stock characters and ironic types
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters like Avidienus, Scaeva, Nomentanus, Umbrenus, Trausius are used as types (avaricious, spendthrift, unlucky tenant) to personify follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create or invoke stock names/types whose reputations embody the vice you wish to critique; their repeated traits make the satirical point sharper and allow comedic recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend moral teaching with entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem combines serious moral argument (e.g., value of frugal living, dangers of luxury) with entertaining narrative and humor so the lesson is instructive yet pleasurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for didactic content to be pleasurable: intersperse sententiae, anecdotes, and wit so readers learn without feeling lectured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ classical allusion and learned parallels for authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's lines 'reproduce some ideas found in the letter of Epicurus to Menoecus' and echo Cicero and Lucretius; phrasing (e.g., tenuis victus) is Ciceronian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor arguments with learned allusion and verbal echoes of canonical authors to lend gravitas and to position the satire within a classical tradition; but use such allusions to illuminate rather than obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace expository passages with rhetorical variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Long discourses are interspersed with questions, anecdotes, contrasts, and hortatory addresses (e.g., 'Learn from me', rhetorical questions about the future).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monotonous exposition: vary sentence rhythm, include rhetorical questions, direct addresses, and short illustrative episodes to maintain interest and rhetorical force.
